01

Overview

Nomad is a location-based discovery app for the moment before plans happen. Instead of another list of “popular near you”, it asks a few useful questions — what you're into, what you want to spend, how far you'll go, who you're with — and returns a short set of places that actually fit.

  • Context over categories

    Mood, budget, distance and company shape the results — not just cuisine or category.

  • Fewer, better options

    A shortlist designed to be decided on, rather than an infinite scroll.

  • Built for groups

    Preferences can be combined, so nobody has to negotiate through the app.

02

The problem

Discovery is fragmented by default. People move between Maps, TikTok, Reddit, review sites and group chats, then rebuild one decision from five sources. Existing apps either surface generic popularity or hand the filtering work straight back to the user.

“I know what kind of experience I want, but it's hard to find the right places without spending a lot of time searching.”

User interview · Nomad research
03

Research

01

6 user interviews

Travellers and locals who go out regularly — from spontaneous students to parents planning family trips.

02

8 platforms benchmarked

Google Maps, Yelp, TripAdvisor, TikTok, Instagram, Reddit, ChatGPT and Airbnb Experiences.

03

Synthesis

Affinity mapping across interviews and teardowns, distilled into four core insights and three behavioural archetypes.

What I heard

  • 01

    People scan visually. Photos, price and distance are the first filter — ratings come after.

  • 02

    Budget and travel distance decide more visits than popularity does.

  • 03

    Recommendations only feel personal when the context is explicit: mood, occasion, group.

  • 04

    Too many options reads as “no answer”, not as freedom.

04

Who I designed for

Three behavioural archetypes, built from the interviews rather than from demographics alone.

23 · Student

Social Explorer

“I want to find unique places that match my interests and mood without spending hours searching.”
  • Explores new cities
  • Loves cafés, local culture and photography
  • Prefers budget-friendly options

28 · Working professional

Intentional Planner

“We want curated recommendations that fit our budget and give us a great experience.”
  • Plans weekend getaways
  • Looks for scenic spots and activities
  • Wants easy planning and trustworthy recommendations

22–26 · Graduate student

Context-Driven Seeker

“We want fun places and activities that are easy to plan for our group.”
  • Explores new places together
  • Looks for group-friendly spots
  • Filters by budget, distance and activity type
05

What the research changed

01

Discovery is fragmented

People jump between four or five apps to decide on one place. The opportunity isn't another source — it's the place where the decision happens.

02

Relevance beats abundance

A shorter list that fits the moment is more useful than an exhaustive one.

03

Discovery isn't decision

Reviews, photos, price, hours and distance are what turn interest into a plan.

04

Popularity creates inspiration. Trust creates action.

Trending places get attention, but people book what they can verify.

06

Ideation & design process

  1. 01

    Brainstorming

    Explored different ways to help people find a relevant experience quickly.

  2. 02

    Information architecture

    Built a simple structure for filtering, browsing and saving.

  3. 03

    Low-fidelity wireframes

    Iterated on layout to test hierarchy and navigation before visual design.

  4. 04

    High-fidelity design

    A warm, travel-inspired system with photography, soft surfaces and clear states.

Low-fidelity wireframes

07

Final design

A clean, warm interface that makes discovering and comparing places feel like planning a trip — not filing a report.

Impact

What changed

4
Core insights from 6 interviews and 8 platforms

Findings from moderated usability testing and design review. These are qualitative signals from a small test group, not production analytics.

09

Learnings

01

Context is the product

Understanding mood, group and budget produced more relevant recommendations than adding more filters.

02

Iterate on evidence

Usability testing surfaced friction I couldn't see in the file — five rounds of changes followed.

03

Design for range

Flexible filters kept Nomad useful for a student spending $20 and a family planning a week away.
